title: A Undertow for the Inventory
premise: Ansel Crane, a woman who has spent a decade writing postcards to her dead mother's burned-down house, works as an invisible archivist in a coastal city's records office. When Maren Oduya, the last fluent speaker of Kivunji, a language brought by island laborers two generations ago, asks Ansel to become her final student, Ansel is forced out of her self-imposed erasure and into the role of witness, translator, and heir. As Maren's health fails and city officials move to demolish the last Kivunji meeting hall, Ansel must choose between retreating into silence and speaking the language aloud at a public hearing—knowing that to speak it is to finally grieve her mother, whose letters she never answered. The novel ends with Maren's death, the hall's demolition, and Ansel recording the first Kivunji lesson for a stranger's child: survival, she learns, is not keeping things intact but passing them on broken.
about_author: Ivo Dunmore is the pen name of a former municipal archivist who spent eleven years cataloguing the papers of vanished immigrant societies before turning to fiction. They live in a port town where three languages are spoken in one kitchen, and they write about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. We meet her routines: the postcards addressed to a lot where nothing stands, the filing room where she corrects other people's names and no one knows hers. Emotional beat: the eerie comfort of being unrecorded.

chapters.title: Postcards to Ash
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. A flashback braided through present-day mail sorting reveals the fire, her unanswered final letter to her mother, and why she writes to an address instead of a grave. Beat: guilt disguised as habit.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Counts Backward
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. At the harbor library she notices Maren Oduya, elderly and sharp, reciting numbers in an unknown tongue to keep them alive. Their first exchange is brusque; Maren calls Ansel 'the girl who files people.' Beat: reluctant recognition.

chapters.title: Kivunji
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. She explains the language of her island childhood, brought by contract laborers, now spoken by exactly one person. She has been auditioning strangers for years and failing them. Beat: the loneliness of being a whole civilization.

chapters.title: One Final Student
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Maren asks Ansel directly; Ansel refuses, citing work, then lies awake composing refusals in her head like letters. Beat: terror of being needed.

chapters.title: The Hall on Delacroix Street
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel visits the crumbling Kivunji meeting hall out of curiosity and finds demolition notices posted by the city's redevelopment office—her own office's paperwork. Beat: complicity discovered.

chapters.title: First Lesson
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Ansel returns, not quite agreeing, and Maren begins teaching anyway: greetings, the word for tide, the word for 'left behind.' Ansel's mouth resists the sounds. Beat: the body's stubborn grief.

chapters.title: Inventory of Small Losses
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. At work, Ansel quietly misfiles the demolition order, buying time, and understands she has crossed a line. Her supervisor Voss grows suspicious. Beat: power tasted for the first time.

chapters.title: What the Tide Keeps
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren tells the story of the 1954 flood, when Kivunji speakers saved neighbors who later banned their language from schoolyards. Beat: bitterness as inheritance.

chapters.title: Voss
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Voss confronts Ansel over the misfiled document; she deflects, but he offers a bargain—her silence about the hall's structural report in exchange for his silence about hers. Beat: corruption begins politely.

chapters.title: The Grammar of Goodbye
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Lessons deepen: Kivunji has no future tense, only an 'arriving' form. Maren reveals she is dying and has perhaps a season left. Beat: urgency sharpened into tenderness.

chapters.title: Letters Never Answered
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Maren finds one of Ansel's postcards and reads it aloud, gently, in both languages. Ansel storms out, then sits all night on the seawall unable to write a new one. Beat: the armor cracks.

chapters.title: The Hearing Notice
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The demolition moves up on the calendar; a public comment period opens. Voss pressures Ansel to stay invisible. For the first time she imagines speaking—at a microphone, in Kivunji. Beat: fear becoming want.

chapters.title: Chorus of the Almost-Gone
chapters.summary: Multiple short POVs. Descendants of Kivunji families react to the notice: some shrug, one old man weeps, a teenage girl named Priya asks what the words mean. Beat: a community discovering its own ghost.

chapters.title: Priya
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Priya shows up at Maren's door asking to learn; Maren, exhausted, hesitates—too little time, too many failures. Ansel advocates for her, surprising herself. Beat: Ansel becomes a keeper rather than a tenant.

chapters.title: The Structural Report
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel discovers Voss falsified the hall's inspection to speed demolition for a donor's project. She copies the real report. Beat: the price of survival made explicit—exposure means losing everything.

chapters.title: Arriving Tense
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Hospitalized after a fall, Maren dictates vocabulary to Ansel from bed, racing memory loss. She makes Ansel promise to speak at the hearing—not for the building, for the language. Beat: a deathbed that refuses melodrama.

chapters.title: Everything Filed Under Miscellaneous
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Voss finds the copied report and threatens termination and prosecution. Alone in the archive at night, Ansel addresses her mother aloud for the first time, in fragments of Kivunji. Beat: the lowest point and the turn.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV (climax). Before the council, Ansel produces the falsified report, then abandons her prepared statement and speaks in Kivunji—the language arriving in a public room for the first time in decades. Priya repeats the words. The hall is granted a stay; Voss resigns. Beat: voice breaking open like weather.

chapters.title: Tide Word
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren, released home, hears recordings of the hearing and laughs until she cries. She teaches Priya and Ansel together, correcting them with renewed ferocity. Beat: joy as a form of reckoning.

chapters.title: The Last Speaker, No Longer
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren dies on an ordinary morning mid-lesson, mid-word. Ansel finishes the sentence for her. The community holds a service conducted half in Kivunji, badly, beautifully. Beat: grief performed out loud at last.

chapters.title: A Undertow for the Inventory
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel mails her final postcard—to Priya's address, not the burned lot—and begins recording lessons for anyone who wants them. She signs her full name to the archive's new Kivunji collection. Beat: ownership claimed; survival as transmission.
